title: The Shop on Juan Flórez Where a Dressing-Gown Maker Became Zara
dek: In May 1975 Amancio Ortega and Rosalía Mera, who had spent about twelve years making clothes for other shops, opened one of their own in A Coruña.

story.event: Opening the first Zara shop on Juan Flórez street in A Coruña
story.summary: On 9 May 1975 Amancio Ortega and Rosalía Mera, whose workshop Confecciones GOA had made dressing gowns and lingerie for other retailers since about 1963, opened their own shop, Zara, at 64-66 Juan Flórez in A Coruña. Accounts differ on why: a 2004 Harvard Business Review article says a cancelled German lingerie order forced the move, while WWD described a deliberate shift to selling direct. The shop traded until January 2026.
paragraphs: On 9 May 1975 a clothes shop opened at numbers 64 and 66 of Juan Flórez street in A Coruña, in Galicia. Its owners were not new to clothing. Amancio Ortega and Rosalía Mera had met as young employees of La Maja, a fashion shop in the city; Mera had left school at 11 to work as a seamstress. Since about 1963 they had run Confecciones GOA, a workshop making quilted dressing gowns and lingerie for other retailers. Women who knew Mera from those years later recalled her sewing in the basement of the Calle Noya workshop with her baby daughter's basket beside her.

Why they opened a shop is told two ways. In a 2004 Harvard Business Review article, three operations professors wrote that a German wholesaler had suddenly cancelled a large lingerie order, that the company's capital was tied up in it with no other buyer, and that Ortega, fearing bankruptcy, opened a shop near the factory to sell the goods himself. WWD, in its 2013 obituary of Mera, told it as a choice: by the early 1970s the couple had several hundred employees and many retail customers, and realised they would earn more by selling directly. A 2002 El Mundo profile says the founders had long resolved not merely to produce for others but to make, distribute and sell.

They meant to call the shop Zorba, after the film Zorba the Greek, but a bar nearby already had the name. According to the Associated Press and WWD, they rearranged the letters they already had into Zara. The shop sold low-priced versions of popular, more expensive clothes.

Two years later Zara began opening elsewhere in Spain, with a headquarters and factories at Arteixo, outside the city. After the birth of their son Marcos, who has a disability, Mera stepped back from the business and trained as a teacher. In 1986, the year she and Ortega separated, she founded the Paideia Foundation, which worked with disabled people. She died in 2013.

The Juan Flórez shop traded for more than fifty years. Zara closed it on 30 January 2026, with the building reported to be too small for the chain's current format, and planned to move its eleven staff to other shops in the city.

quote.text: the things which we know, any of us, are just those which we can best perform, that is to say, with ease and expedition; it is a joy to do them, and the result is beautiful.
quote.locator: Book II, Chapter VII (Socrates and Aristarchus)
quote.source_title: The Memorabilia, tr. Henry Graham Dakyns, Project Gutenberg eBook #1177
quote.connection: Socrates tells a friend in hard times to start from what his household already knows how to make. Whether the first Zara was forced or planned, it did not ask its founders for a new trade, only for a new place to offer the one they had.

reflection: Nobody agrees on exactly why the shop on Juan Flórez opened, and perhaps both stories hold some truth: a plan can sit in a drawer for years until a bad week makes it urgent. What is not in dispute is what the founders brought to it, about a dozen years of knowing how to make the thing they were selling.
When something you depend on falls through, the reflex is to look for a new idea. Sometimes the steadier move is to look at what you already do well and ask who else might want it, and in what form.
invitation: Write down one thing you can do with ease that others around you find hard. Before the day ends, ask one colleague or friend whether it would be useful to them.

research_notes: Both founders are credited throughout, as the AP and WWD obituaries do. The motive for the shop is genuinely disputed and the story gives both versions with attribution: Harvard Business Review (Ferdows, Lewis and Machuca, 2004) says a German wholesaler's cancelled lingerie order left the 'fledgling' company's capital tied up and that Ortega opened the shop in desperation; WWD (2013) says the couple, with several hundred employees and many retail clients by the early 1970s, chose to sell direct; FashionUnited (2025) frames it as a planned diversification after a decade supplying retailers such as El Corte Inglés; El Mundo (2002) says the founding group had resolved early on to make, distribute and sell. The HBR 'fledgling' description and WWD's 'several hundred employees' are in tension; both are attributed and neither is used as fact. WWD also says Inditex was founded in 1975; the group was formed in 1985 (FashionUnited), so the story does not repeat WWD's date. El Mundo includes Ortega's brother Antonio and his wife Primitiva Renedo among GOA's founders; the story's 'the founders' covers them without naming them. Age at first work: WWD and La Voz say Mera left school at 11 to work as a seamstress; El Mundo says her first job, at La Maja, was at 13; the story uses 11 for leaving school and does not give an age for La Maja. Her son's disability is described as cerebral palsy by El País and as Down syndrome by La Voz; the story says only that he was born with a disability. The basement anecdote is El Mundo's report of what women who knew her from the early years remembered. The closure reason ('too small') is RetailDetail's reporting, so the story says 'reported'. The Hebrew and English Wikipedia articles were used only as a map to sources. The Telegraph (paywall) and Bloomberg (403) obituaries could not be loaded and are not cited. The Socrates passage is advice to Aristarchus about setting his household to work at the crafts they already knew; it is applied here by analogy.
